gist: Atwood argues that the terrifying apparitions and 'demons' met in the Mysteries are products of the soul's own moist, condensed imaginative vehicle, a Hades of images to be passed through unmoved until the soul is dried and purified, and she identifies this chaotic state with the alchemists' First Matter, in whose purified extreme the Seed of Spirit is found. She ends with the start of a Rosicrucian allegory of the guarded mountain reached at night with a guide.

notes.point: Philosophers echo the preceding accounts: Plato likens the soul's descent into the oblivious realms of generation to an earthquake.

Psellus: Chaldaic-rite apparitions include 'superinspection', a light in some form; the oracle forbids heeding it or trusting its voice. Such apparitions come from the soul's passions and have no substance.
The poets veiled this vaporous estate as Pan, who wears monstrous disguises to frighten would-be captors; Virgil's lines on Aeneas and the shades follow (untranslated in the book).

The imaginative spirit makes these images, like dreams but stronger. The humid, condensed pneumatic vehicle forms apparitions as moisture forms clouds; the ancients' demons arise from this vapor. By rapport one meets the whole phantasmagoric universe of one's sphere.

Proclus: material images, even divine-seeming, draw unpurified souls from truth; mystics meet many-shaped forms first, then, unmoved and inside the Temple, receive illumination. Atwood places these images in the evaporative purification, before the inner light.
Basil Valentine: these exterior spirits know arts, including healing, and so trap the imperfect spiritual intellect.

Many authorities describe them: desire vivifies the aerial forms; the oracle allows pure demons and useful products of evil matter; Synesius calls them matter's progeny at war with the soul; Proclus' hymn says they keep souls toiling, forgetful of their origin.
The oracle: keep the eyes upward, away from image-loving Hades.

Porphyry: a soul clinging to nature grows moist, shadowed and heavy; one leaving nature becomes a dry splendor. Heraclitus' dry soul, turned to itself, radiates its own light. Hermes: withdraw the watery nature from the fire until the redness is pure.

The 'earth' holding the Stone is our chaotic sense-life, which rectified becomes a spiritual body. Life is fire imprisoned in aerial moisture; unpurified, that moisture is Hades, the Purgatory of the wise, where consciousness is perplexed and opposing powers clash until union. Phantoms guard the mineral soul.

Vaughan: the First Matter never keeps one shape, driven by the fire of nature, which Atwood parallels with the re-entering Light of Reason, the adepts' Sulfur. Lully's monstrous 'first principles', known by self-inspection, are so called because the Seed of Spirit is found in their purified extreme.

That seed, a heavy star-like ens, is the whole Demogogon not yet animated by its returning light: a hidden 'rock in the wilderness', the viscous soul, the deformed divine germ of humanity, like Glaucus.

A Rosicrucian letter, applied to initiation: an invisible central mountain guarded by beasts, sought on the darkest night with prayer, a self-offering guide and courage, without weapons. Themistus: a conductor opens the vestibule to the perplexed initiate.

method.veiled: These apparitions are created by the passions of the soul, in performing divine rites, mere appearances, having no substance, and therefore not signifying anything true
method.plain: Visions such as lights in various forms that appear during the work come from the operator's own passions. They are insubstantial and must not be trusted or attended to.

also.text: he apply not his mind to it, nor esteem the voice proceeding thence to be true
the first called superinspection, when he who celebrates the divine rites sees a mere apparition, as, for instance, of light in some form or figure

method.veiled: the poets also fabulously concealed under the satiric form of Pan, who exhibited himself in every variety of atrocious disguises of wild beasts, and monsters, and demoniacal appearances, that he might affright those who would captivate him
method.plain: Pan stands for the 'vaporous estate of universal-being', which shows itself in frightening shapes that deter whoever tries to grasp it.

also.text: Monstrum, horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptu.

method.veiled: For it is the imaginative spirit which is the maker of these images, as in dreams, only more intense
method.plain: The imaginative faculty itself produces the visions and 'demons'. They work like dreams but are stronger.

also.text: from an included vapor of the imagination

method.veiled: our pneumatic vehicle, becoming humid and condensed beneath her heaven, presents many formidable apparitions to the inner sense
method.plain: When the soul's subtle vehicle is moist and condensed, it throws up apparitions to the inner sense, just as condensed moisture forms clouds that the wind shapes.

also.text: the soul looking at things posterior to herself beholds the shadow and images of her vaporous vehicle

method.veiled: each by rapport in this state becomes conversant with the whole phantasmagoric universe of his sphere
method.plain: In this state the person perceives, through rapport, the whole image-world of his sphere and not only his own images. This explains the crowded imagery of the accounts.

method.veiled: material images, assuming the appearance even of things divine, constantly attended on the Mysteries, drawing towards them souls not yet sufficiently purified, and separating them from truth
method.plain: Some deceptive images even look divine. They pull an insufficiently purified soul away from truth and toward matter.

also.text: the impulsive forms of certain terrestrial demons appear, which call the attention off from undefiled advantages to matter

method.veiled: on entering the interior part of the Temple, unmoved and guarded by the sacred rites, they genuinely receive into their bosom divine illumination
method.plain: The order is fixed: many-shaped phantoms come first. Only a soul that stays unmoved by them and goes further inward receives true illumination. Atwood places the phantoms during purification and before the vision of the inner light.

also.text: during the evaporative process of purification, and before the lucid vision of the light within
the mystics at first meet with the multiform and many-shaped genera which are hurled forth before the gods

method.veiled: the evaporative process of purification
method.plain: Purification works as a drying: the moist vapor of the soul's vehicle, which breeds images, is driven off.
method.basis: II.3 ¶22 links the images to 'an included vapor' and a humid, condensed vehicle. II.3 ¶27 says the soul that leaves nature 'becomes a dry splendor' and that 'a dry soul is the wisest'.

method.veiled: the spiritual also, not et perfected, is liable to be caught in the traps of these exterior spirits
method.plain: An imperfect spiritual faculty can be captured by these spirits. Citing Basil Valentine, Atwood says they seem intelligent, skilled and even able to heal, and that this is how they divert the seeker from better things.

also.text: endowed with senses and understanding, know Arts, and have in themselves an occult operative life
by which they deceive and detain the unwary from the search of better things

method.veiled: desire, entering into those aerial forms, is said to vivify them
method.plain: Desire entering the aerial forms is said to give them life and effect. The chunk does not say whose desire.
method.voice: QUOTED: Psellus, Proclus, Iamblicus, Porphyry (as reported by Atwood)

method.veiled: and that the germinations even of evil matter are of use
method.plain: The products of impure matter are not wholly worthless and can serve a use. The chunk does not say what use.

also.text: the Chaldaic oracle even persuades that there are pure demons

method.veiled: Let the immortal depth of thy soul be predominant, and all thy eyes extend upwards
method.plain: Keep the deepest part of the soul in command and direct all attention upward. Do not turn toward the image-filled dark world.

also.text: incline not to the dark world whose depth is a faithless bottom and Hades dark all over, squalid, delighting in images

method.veiled: it attracts moisture when it continually endeavors to associate with nature, whose operations are effected in moisture
method.plain: The soul becomes moist, heavy and image-bound because it keeps clinging to nature.

also.text: If the soul on its departure, says Porphyry, still possesses a spirit turbid from humid exhalations, it then attracts to itself a shadow and becomes heavy

method.veiled: when however the soul earnestly desires to depart from nature (i.e., strives to penetrate centrally without exploring the intermediate spheres), then she becomes a dry splendor from exhalation
method.plain: The cure is a direct turn inward to the center, without lingering in the intermediate spheres of images. This dries the soul and makes it luminous. The parenthesis glosses 'depart from nature'.
method.voice: QUOTED: Porphyry, with Atwood's parenthetical gloss

also.text: a dry soul is the wisest

method.veiled: when she is converted to herself, she evolves her proper essence and irradiates the whole circumference with her own abundant oxygenating and dispersive light
method.plain: When the soul turns to itself, it unfolds its own essence and lights its whole sphere with its own light, instead of seeing shadows.
method.voice: UNCLEAR (follows Heraclitus' saying; n30 cites Proclus)

method.veiled: take, my son, this watery and corrupted nature, which is as a coal holding the fire, which if thou salt withdraw so often until the redness is made pure
method.plain: Repeatedly separate the watery, obscuring element from the fire it holds until that fire, the 'redness', is pure. It then unites with the operator.
method.basis: II.3 ¶27 introduces Hermes with 'Thus' directly after Porphyry and Heraclitus on drying the moist spirit, so the 'watery' part is read as the soul's moisture. The 'clouds' over the ray echo the cloud image for the vapor in II.3 ¶22.

also.text: Extract from the ray its shadow and its obscurity, by which the clouds hang over it, and corrupt and keep away the light
then it will associate with thee, by whom it was cherished and in whom it rests

method.veiled: not the feculent dead soil, but our dark divulsed chaotic life from sense, which opened and rectified, dissolved and reunited, is changed from an earthly to a spiritual body, by rapport divine
method.plain: The 'earth' whose interior holds the Stone is the operator's own disordered sense-life, not literal soil. The steps are: open it, rectify it, dissolve it, reunite it. It then becomes a spiritual body through divine rapport.

also.text: Visit the interior of the earth rectifying, says the sage, and thou shalt find the hidden Stone, the true medicine

method.veiled: the life of all things here below to be a thick fire imprisoned in a certain incombustible aerial moisture
method.plain: Life is a fire held inside a moisture. Atwood says alchemists found this by experiment, passing through the animal and vegetable into the mineral circulation of nature's Law.

also.text: Ignis rubber super dorsum ignis candidi

method.veiled: which moisture in its native state, before it is purified by the inflowing light of reason, is that Hades we are treating of, the Purgatory of the wise
method.plain: The unpurified moisture is the Hades of the Mysteries. It is a stage in which the consciousness is anxious, perplexed and unable on its own to see the reality it aims at.

also.text: wherein the consciousness, becoming artificially wrapped by the Mysteries, continues for a while in a state of solicitude and painful amazement
unable of itself to discover, through so great a cloud of darkness, that Hypostatic Reality towards which it is instructed evermore to aspire
the initiated is seized at first with solicitude and perplexity, unable to move a step forward

method.veiled: until this attraction is found and finally established in union, the opposive powers display their mutual forces in discordant dissolute array
method.plain: The conflict of opposing forces lasts until the attraction to the Hypostatic Reality is found and fixed in union.

method.veiled: the many real, though chimerical horrors and enticing phantoms that haunt around, guarding the secret chamber of their mineral soul
method.plain: Terrifying and alluring phantoms surround the inner 'mineral soul'. They are real as experiences but illusory, and the alchemists warn how to conduct oneself among them.

also.text: there is an angel standing upon it, and that angel struggles to prevail
is compassed about with very cruel beasts and ravenous birds, which make the way thither both difficult and dangerous

method.veiled: the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries, which is that Sulfur of adepts, causing all this manifold scenery in the disruption of life
method.plain: The adepts' 'Sulfur' is the Light of Reason re-entering the soul. As it enters, it breaks up the life and causes the changing scenery of images. It also purifies the moisture.

also.text: before it is purified by the inflowing light of reason

method.veiled: The eye of man never saw her twice under one and the same shape
method.plain: The First Matter never holds one form. Like wind-driven clouds, it keeps changing shape under the 'fire of nature', which Atwood sets in parallel with the re-entering Light of Reason.

also.text: so is she persecuted by the fire of nature
certain fugitive spirits condensed in the air, in shape of divers monsters, beasts, and men, which move like clouds hither and thither

method.veiled: Our Stone comes with light and with light it is generated, and then it brings forth the clouds, and darkness which is the mother of all things
method.plain: Light both generates the Stone and brings on the clouds and darkness, so the cloudy phase is a product of the light entering.
method.basis: In II.3 ¶30 the quote directly follows Atwood's statement that the re-entering Light of Reason causes 'all this manifold scenery'. The chunk does not explain the saying further.

also.text: which containest and separatest all things in a middle principle

method.veiled: as from the self-inspection of them in life
method.plain: Lully's monster-shaped 'first principles' would be absurd if taken outwardly. Atwood holds they were known by inspecting one's own inner life.

method.veiled: within the material extreme of this life, when it is purified, the Seed of Spirit is at last found
method.plain: The chaotic forms are called 'first principles' only because, once the lowest material level of this life is purified, the Seed of Spirit is found within it.

also.text: not because they are permanent or their essence rational, in that unctuous dark condition

method.veiled: a decompounded ens, extremely heavy, shining through the darkness like a fiery star, being full of eyes like pearls or aglets
method.plain: This is how the found Seed appears: heavy, decompounded and shining like a star in the darkness, full of eye-like points. The chunk gives no further explanation.

method.veiled: For it is the whole Demogogon, as yet not actually animated by contact of his own returning light
method.plain: What is found is the whole being in potential, not yet brought to life because its own light has not yet returned to it.
method.basis: II.3 ¶30 follows the description of the Seed of Spirit and links 'returning light' with the 're-entering Light of Reason' earlier in the same paragraph. The referent of 'it' is uncertain (see ambiguities).

also.text: The father of it, says Vaughan, is a certain inviolable mass

method.veiled: In such a deplorable condition is the divine germ of humanity said to be beheld under the thousand evils of its birth
method.plain: In its raw state the subject is the divine germ in humanity, overgrown and deformed like Plato's Glaucus, and hard to find, like a 'rock in the wilderness'.

also.text: This is the rock in the wilderness,, because in great obscurity and difficult to find the way of
Our viscous soul, as Synesius calls it, circulating in the midst of all her Adamical defilements

method.veiled: There is a mountain situated in the midst of the earth or center of the world, which is both small and great
method.plain: The goal of initiatory progress is a hidden, central place of treasure: paradoxical, invisible and guarded. It is reached only through the worthy person's own labor.
method.basis: II.3 ¶31: Atwood says the letter 'appears to have reference to this passage of initiatory progress in the Mysteries'. II.3 ¶32 adds 'it is invisible' and 'only by the worthy man’s self-labor and investigation'. Its central placement parallels 'penetrate centrally' in II.3 ¶27.
method.voice: QUOTED: Brethren of the Rosy Cross (applied by Atwood)

also.text: but, by the providence of God, it is invisible
but only by the worthy man’s self-labor and investigation

method.veiled: It is necessary that you arm yourself with a resolute heroic courage, lest you fear those things that will happen and fall back
method.plain: The operator must prepare by prayer, go in the deepest darkness, and have firm courage so as not to retreat from what will happen. No physical means are needed, only sincere seeking of God.
method.voice: QUOTED: Brethren of the Rosy Cross (applied by Atwood)

also.text: To this mountain you should go in a certain night, when it comes most long and dark; and see that you prepare yourself by prayer
You need no sword or other bodily weapon, only call upon you God, sincerely and heartily seeking Him

method.veiled: ask not of any man where it lies; only follow your guide who will offer himself to you and will meet you in the way
method.plain: A guide appears on the way, unasked, and is to be followed. The footnote compares him to the conductor who opens the vestibule to the perplexed initiate, and to the light promised to one who approaches the fire. The chunk does not identify the guide.
method.voice: QUOTED: Brethren of the Rosy Cross (applied by Atwood)

also.text: till the conductor laying open for him the vestibule, he enters
the Chaldaic oracle promises that the mortal, approaching the fire, will have a light from divinity

quotes.text: the first called superinspection, when he who celebrates the divine rites sees a mere apparition

beholds the shadow and images of her vaporous vehicle

terms.meaning: A connection by which the person in this state meets the whole image-world of his sphere. The change to a spiritual body happens 'by rapport divine'.

terms.meaning: Apparitional beings arising from the enclosed vapor of imagination. They are called progeny of matter and are said to have sense, arts and an operative life, which they use to deceive. They are vivified by desire and are at war with the truth-seeking soul. The Chaldaic oracle also speaks of 'pure demons'.

quotes.text: all the race of demons, so much celebrated by antiquity, appear to have their origin in a life of this kind, viz., from an included vapor of the imagination
as the progeny of matter, and as having an energetic virtue, but at natural war with the truth-seeking soul

terms.meaning: The term is used once, in connection with the material images seen during the evaporative purification. Its referent is unclear (see ambiguities).

quotes.text: And that such actually appeared to be the Musai, during the evaporative process of purification

terms.meaning: Contemplation in which, according to Proclus, the same order holds as in the Mysteries: phantasms first, illumination later.

quotes.text: the same method takes place in the speculation of Wholes

terms.meaning: The dark, image-loving lower world, and the aerial moisture of life in its unpurified state. In it, consciousness wrapped by the Mysteries is anxious and perplexed.

equivalences.quote: is that Hades we are treating of, the Purgatory of the wise

equivalences.quote: which moisture in its native state, before it is purified by the inflowing light of reason, is that Hades we are treating of

terms.meaning: The state of a soul that has left nature and its moisture. It turns to itself and radiates its own light. Heraclitus calls it the wisest.

quotes.text: then she becomes a dry splendor from exhalation
a dry soul is the wisest

equivalences.quote: thou shalt find the hidden Stone, the true medicine

terms.meaning: The incombustible moisture in which the thick fire of life is imprisoned. Unpurified, it is Hades.

quotes.text: a thick fire imprisoned in a certain incombustible aerial moisture

terms.meaning: What the consciousness in Hades is taught to aspire to but cannot find by itself through the darkness.

quotes.text: that Hypostatic Reality towards which it is instructed evermore to aspire

terms.meaning: The inner 'secret chamber' that horrors and phantoms guard.

equivalences.quote: the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries, which is that Sulfur of adepts

equivalences.quote: the re-entering Light of Reason in the Mysteries, which is that Sulfur of adepts

ambiguities.quote: And that such actually appeared to be the Musai
readings: The 'Musai' are the material images or demons that appear during purification.
The 'Musai' are the initiates to whom such images appeared.
ambiguities.basis: Grammatically, 'such' (the material images) 'appeared to be the Musai', which supports reading 1. The Proclus passage that follows speaks of 'the mystics' meeting these forms, which could support reading 2.

readings: As printed: the mystics are 'divested' of something on receiving illumination.
The phrase is hard to reconcile with receiving 'divine illumination' in the same clause and may be corrupt; the intended sense is unclear.
ambiguities.basis: II.3 ¶22: the phrase immediately follows 'they genuinely receive into their bosom divine illumination'.

ambiguities.quote: For it is the whole Demogogon
readings: 'it' is the Seed of Spirit / decompounded ens just described.
'it' is the chaotic material extreme of life as a whole.
ambiguities.basis: The sentence follows the ens description directly, which supports reading 1. 'the whole' and 'not yet animated' fit the unpurified chaotic forms discussed just before, which supports reading 2.

ambiguities.quote: This is the rock in the wilderness,, because in great obscurity
readings: 'This' is Vaughan's 'inviolable mass', the father of it.
'This' is the Seed / Demogogon. The following 'Our viscous soul' stands in apposition and names the same thing.
ambiguities.basis: The phrase directly follows the Vaughan quote, which supports reading 1. The dash and 'Our viscous soul ... In such a deplorable condition is the divine germ' tie it to the soul or germ, which supports reading 2.

ambiguities.quote: Ignis rubber super dorsum ignis candidi
readings: It restates the preceding image: a red fire (the thick fire of life) carried on a white fire (the moisture).
It is a separate emblem the text does not explain.
ambiguities.basis: In II.3 ¶29 it is set off with dashes right after 'a thick fire imprisoned in a certain incombustible aerial moisture'. No gloss is given.

translations.original: Corripit hic subita trepidus formidine ferrum Aeneas strictamque aciem venientibus offert. Et ni docta comes tenues sine corpore vitas Admoneat volitare cava sub imagine formae, Irruat, et frustra ferro diverberet umbras
translations.translation: Here Aeneas, trembling with sudden fear, seizes his sword and turns the drawn edge on those approaching. Had his learned companion not warned him that these were thin, bodiless lives flitting under a hollow semblance of form, he would rush in and vainly cleave the shades with steel.

translations.original: Natura suadet esse demonas puros, et malae materiae germina utilia et bona
translations.translation: the Chaldaic oracle even persuades that there are pure demons ... and that the germinations even of evil matter are of use

translations.original: Ducat animae profunditas immortalis oculosque affatim, --- Omnes sursum extende.
translations.translation: Let the immortal depth of thy soul be predominant, and all thy eyes extend upwards

translations.original: Umbrarum hic locus est, somni noctisque soporae
translations.translation: This is the place of shades, of sleep and of drowsy night.

translations.original: Visitabis interiora terrae rectificando, invneies Occultum lapidem, veram medicianam.
translations.translation: Visit the interior of the earth rectifying, says the sage, and thou shalt find the hidden Stone, the true medicine

translations.original: Ignis rubber super dorsum ignis candidi
translations.translation: Red fire upon the back of white fire.

translations.original: Spiritus fugitives in aero condensators, in forma monstrorum diversorum et animalium etiam hominum, qui vadunt sicut nubes, modo hinc modo illuc
translations.translation: certain fugitive spirits condensed in the air, in shape of divers monsters, beasts, and men, which move like clouds hither and thither

translations.original: Monstrum, horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptu.
translations.translation: A monster, dreadful, shapeless, huge, whose light (sight) has been taken away.

translations.original: Nunc animis opus, Aenea, nunc pectore firmo.
translations.translation: Now there is need of courage, Aeneas, now of a steadfast heart.

threads.note: 'And all this, extravagant and fanciful though it should appear' refers back to the preceding account of the convulsions and apparitions at the Mysteries, which is not in this chunk.
'that Hades we are treating of' points to an earlier discussion of Hades.
Vaughan 'notes the same in the Regio Phantastica of his Hieroglyphic, and elsewhere', pointing to Vaughan's works outside this chunk.
The Rosicrucian letter 'appears to have reference to this passage of initiatory progress in the Mysteries', tying it to the stage just described. The letter continues past the end of this chunk.

'The adepts, many of them, are at some pains to denote the peculiar disposition and appearance of this guide' points to fuller treatments of the guide elsewhere. 'See Warburton’s Divine Legation' gives the source for Themistus.
